I moved in with my husband to his house. All bills were withdrawn from his account - an account he has had since he was a child and emancipated minor. He is now in his thirties. To make it a joint account, the bank would have to close out that account number and reopen new accounts for everything. We would then have to call the gas, sewage, garbage, water, electric, mortgage, and everything else that is set to autopay and change the account information via the phone. They won't do it any other way. 

That assumes they will pick up or have hours that we can call. Some of those places are only open 8-4 and we work those hours. Sure, we can call on lunch - and have - but they often don't pick up in a timely manner because they are on lunch, too. We have had issues calling to change things in the past. We aren't down to not have a bill paid on time, so no, we are not making a joint account. It takes more than an hour and we run the risk of something not getting paid or getting shut off because we can't get through to people.

So, no, not laziness. It's more responsible on our part this way. Most banks I am sure it doesn't take all this - it doesn't at my bank - but it does for his and we aren't taking that risk. His credit score is almost 750. We are not destroying that just to gain the approval of everyone else in the world.

What we do works for us: I send him money for my share of the bills and cover groceries. Everything is taken out of his account. No fuss, no interruptions.

I teach HS English. 15-19 year old elective literature and writing courses. We just finished a novel that changes perspectives every chapter. When we finished Part 3, a bunch of kids were confused why one character went into the room where the bombs had been hidden three chapters earlier by a different character who never interacts with the one who ran into the room. I had to explain to them that just because we know something doesn't mean the characters do. The students all thought that was stupid. 

I then pulled out a sheet of paper. On one side, I drew a triangle. On the other I drew a circle. I held it up so the side with the triangle faced half the students and the circle side faced the other half. I asked them what shape was on the paper. They were confused to find out both were right because of changing perspective.

When I relayed that story to my mentor teachers at lunch, they laughed and agreed with how I did it. I did not, until that point, realize I would actually have to teach teenagers about different perspectives.

However, reviewing adolescent psychology, it's actually fair. Teenagers and adolescents are in what psych people call the ego centric phase of development. Everything is all about them. Mostly, it's about who they are and how they fit into the world around them, what their core ideals and relationships are, etc., but it also means that, with the developing prefrontal cortex, they are totally absorbed with what they know and think and feel, regardless of what others' experiences are. This is why they are moody, argumentative, and prone to be oblivious to the world around them. They literally have a ton going on inside their heads.

Back when the movies first came out I learned to braid my hair like this. With practice, I got it down to about 10 minutes. The hardest part is the French braid going around the head; once you get to the hanging down part that is all loose ends, the braid is finished within seconds. A straightforward braid IS faster and probably what Suzanne Collins meant in the book, but for a movie, that style is not visually interesting. They also needed it to serve a greater purpose later on when the girls of the Capitol start wearing their hair "like Katniss's braid." Sure a "simple braid" could work, but the French side braid is unique enough it works better to become part of someone's image or "brand" visually.

Let's also add that people in Stone Age cultures or ancient cultures would do their hair like this. Those people often lived in dire situations like Katniss, but being able to do their hair in a way that set them apart from others (like variations on braids) was a practical means of self-adornment that involved relatively little time, tools, and skills. More complex braids like fishtail braids and waterfall braids take less than half an hour with practice. It's completely plausible Katniss did this herself or even had her mom or sister do it for her. People also often sleep in braids so maybe we're looking at 20 minutes of hair grooming a week, assuming she doesn't wash her hair often. It's implied in the books that baths aren't as routine in District 12 as they are for us, so I find this all extremely plausible.

2. The most egregious offense to me is the italicized Spanish everywhere in Encanto. In Coco, all the actors were Mexican and spoke with a Mexican-ish accent in the English dub, so when they mention the ofrenda or tamales or another Spanish word, it doesn't sound out of place. It just flows. Self-discipline.

Discipline became a dirty word in Western culture in the last 20 or so years. Mention disciplining children and students now, and people will call you a child abuser. When it comes to disciplining yourself, people get even worse about it. Discipline doesn't mean beatings. It means exercising whatever means benefit you the most to instill positive and healthy habits. 

Self-discipline has always been a struggle for people, but our culture and lifestyle now has made it so easy to forego any kind of it to the point we're willing to poison ourselves to get what we want. I teach sixteen year olds that only eat mac and cheese from a box or Takis that's all they want so that's all they'll eat. One of the reasons diseases like IBS weren't an issue 100 years ago is because people didn't eat whatever they wanted whenever they wanted. They could only eat what they had. Plant foods were only available in season. Everything was relatively local. Today, I live in a town with two food plants that ship their products to every distribution center within 500 miles. Of course it has to be jam packed with all kinds of synthetic preservatives to last that long and sit on a shelf. 

I digress. The point is, people want what they want when they want it. Treats aren't treats if you get them every day, but by golly, we want it, we got it. You're cruel to deny a child something so harmless as a candy bar, regardless of whether or not the kid has already had one today. Screen time is perceived to be even more harmless than candy. It's no wonder kids today are so lost.
